name: AWS Step Functions
oneLiner: Serverless workflow orchestration as state machines across AWS services.
whatItIs: Step Functions is AWS's serverless orchestration service. You define a workflow as a state machine — a sequence of steps with branching, parallelism, retries, error handling and waits — and Step Functions runs it, calling Lambda functions and 200+ AWS services directly, tracking state and showing a visual execution graph. Unlike Airflow (MWAA), there's no server to run: you pay per state transition and it scales automatically. It's ideal for event-driven and application-style orchestration — coordinating a pipeline's steps, retrying failures, and reacting to events — where a full Airflow environment would be heavyweight.

inPractice.narrative: A file lands in S3 and needs a multi-step process: validate, run a Glue job, wait for it, then load Redshift and notify — with retries if any step fails. A Step Functions state machine models exactly that flow, invoking each service in turn, handling waits and errors, and surfacing a visual trace of every execution. No orchestration server runs between events; it wakes on the trigger and bills per transition. Step Functions is the serverless conductor for event-driven pipelines.

coreConcepts.detail: A workflow defined as states (task, choice, parallel, map, wait, pass, fail) using Amazon States Language (JSON) — with a visual editor (Workflow Studio).
Steps can call 200+ AWS services (Lambda, Glue, ECS, DynamoDB, SNS, etc.) directly without glue code, plus the SDK integrations for fine-grained calls.
Per-state retries with backoff, catch/fallback branches and timeouts make robust, self-healing workflows declarative rather than hand-coded.
Standard workflows are durable and long-running (up to a year), billed per transition; Express workflows are high-volume, short-lived and billed by count/duration — pick by workload.
Parallel branches and Map (including distributed Map over large datasets) fan work out, enabling scalable batch orchestration.
Wait states and task tokens let a workflow pause for human approval or an external system to signal back before continuing.

whenToUse: Event-driven orchestration of AWS services without running a server.
Coordinating pipeline steps with retries, branching and error handling.
Fan-out batch processing via Map/parallel states.
Lightweight orchestration where full Airflow (MWAA) is overkill.
whenNotToUse: Rich data-pipeline scheduling with a DAG ecosystem and backfills — MWAA/Airflow fits better.
Heavy data transformation inside the orchestrator — call Glue/EMR for that.
Complex Python-defined pipelines teams already run in Airflow.
Simple single-function triggers — EventBridge + Lambda may suffice.

keyFacts.label: Definition
keyFacts.value: Amazon States Language (JSON) + visual Workflow Studio.

keyFacts.label: Billing
keyFacts.value: Standard: per state transition; Express: per run + duration.

pricingShape: Standard workflows bill per state transition — each step executed — so cost scales with how many steps run, not idle time (there's no server). Express workflows, for high-volume short flows, bill by number of executions and their duration/memory, which is far cheaper at scale for chatty workflows. Downstream services (Lambda, Glue) are billed separately. The levers are choosing Standard vs Express by volume/duration, and not exploding transition counts with overly granular states. Because it's serverless, an idle workflow costs nothing.
gotchas: Standard bills per transition — very chatty state machines with many tiny steps add up; consider Express or coarser states.
Choosing the wrong type (Standard vs Express) can be much costlier or hit duration limits — match to the workload.
It orchestrates, it doesn't process — don't cram heavy compute into the workflow; call a service.
It's not Airflow — teams needing DAG scheduling, backfills and a Python ecosystem may prefer MWAA.
Amazon States Language has a learning curve; complex flows get verbose (Workflow Studio helps).

equivalents.name: Cloud Workflows
equivalents.note: Serverless orchestration of GCP services/APIs; YAML/JSON step definitions.
